text:
Going to sleep and waking at consistent times is important for health, safety and performance, according to a consensus statement from a National Sleep Foundation expert panel.

The panel reviewed the research on sleep timing and voted on three questions. They agreed that daily regularity in sleep timing matters for both health and performance. They also agreed that when sleep is too short across the working week, catch-up sleep on days off may be beneficial.

Why this matters across roles: those two findings can sound contradictory, and they point to a useful distinction. Someone short on time for sleep may benefit from a modest catch-up. Someone who lies awake once they get to bed is in a different position, where a steady wake time is part of Australian insomnia guidance.

One practical question: is the problem too little time for sleep, or lying awake when you get there?

Where the evidence stops:
• Most of the studies the panel reviewed were observational, so they show links rather than cause and effect.
• A consensus statement reflects expert agreement on the evidence available, which may change as more trials are done.

Key sources:
Sletten, T. L., Weaver, M. D., Foster, R. G., Gozal, D., Klerman, E. B., Rajaratnam, S. M. W., Roenneberg, T., Takahashi, J. S., Turek, F. W., Vitiello, M. V., Young, M. W., & Czeisler, C. A. (2023). The importance of sleep regularity: A consensus statement of the National Sleep Foundation sleep timing and variability panel. Sleep Health. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sleh.2023.07.016
